new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the penultimate syllable of the word; a small number of lexical items carry non-default (contrastive) stress, e.g. final-stressed kaˈwam 'your mouth' vs penult-stressed ˈkawam 'your spouse'.
new_statements.exceptions: 'some examples of contrastive stress to encode semantic difference' — minimal pair /kɑˈwam/ 'your mouth' vs /ˈkɑwam/ 'your spouse'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, unspecified whether citation forms; the only cluster-level primary remark (Lithgow 1976: 475, PTC-wide) says stress is predictable within word classes and shifts one syllable rightward when kin-plural or object suffixes are added, but gives no Ghayavi-specific placement rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Ghayavi = Boianaki/Boanaki (Lithgow 1976: 'Boanaki (Galavi)', coast from Uga to Vidia, centre Boanaki; 75% dialect variation Boanaki-Vidia) = Ray 1907 'Galavi' (Boianai village). Wikipedia's statement does not name a dialect. Glottolog places Ghayavi with Gapapaiwa in a Boanaki-Paiwa node (boan1246); no sister-language statement was used.

new_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress is generally on the penultimate syllable. Sentence level stress is realised by pitch glide and lengthening of the vowel of the stressed syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: First-hand SIL source confirming the catalog's default-penultimate placement (catalog record rests on an unsourced 2023 Wikipedia paragraph). The OPD's 'generally' is compatible with Wikipedia's 'some examples of contrastive stress', but the contrastive minimal pair itself is not in the OPD, so that half of the Wikipedia sentence remains without a located primary source (plausible sources: the unposted Ghayavi Grammar, entry 81957, or the 2001 ADW worksheet/spelling guide the OPD cites). Suggested citation upgrade for the record: McGuckin & Henderson 2001 OPD p. 4 in place of Wikipedia for the penult rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable as the general rule ('generally'); no tone; sentence stress is realised as a pitch glide plus lengthening of the stressed vowel. The transcribed wordlist (pp. 2-4) bears this out: [ˈpoɾo], [boˈnɑɣɑ], [uɾɑtɑˈmɑnɑ], [jɑbuˈmɑnɑ], [uwɑpɑniˈpɑni]; words ending in a diphthong are stressed on the vowel before it ([ˈmɑmɑi], [mɑˈpenɑi], [eˈɡʷɑjɑu], [kuˈɾui], [suˈviɾei]), i.e. a final diphthong counts as one syllable; CVC monosyllable [ˈdɑm].
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described in prose; two long words are transcribed with a secondary stress mark: [didɑˌjoɣʷojoˈɣʷosi] 'children' and [ˌnuɑnuˈɑnɑ] 'mind, heart'; full reduplications are transcribed with two primary stresses: [ˈɡʷeˈɡʷe] 'orphan', [ˈɡouˈɡou] 'owl', [ˈteuˈteu] 'human skull'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated in prose beyond the hedge 'generally'. In the data the interjection aigo 'ouch!' is transcribed with final stress [ɑiˈɡo]; a few forms carry no stress mark ([ɑpɑu] 'cloud', [oke] 'teeth', [ɑgʷɑi] 'cuscus'). The OPD does NOT contain the Wikipedia minimal pair /kɑˈwam/ 'your mouth' vs /ˈkɑwam/ 'your spouse' nor any statement that stress is contrastive.
new_statements.identity_note: Ghayavi [bmk] = Boianaki/Boyanaki (village name; Ray 1907 'Galavi'), Milne Bay Province, north coast of Cape Vogel/Goodenough Bay area; OPD lists major villages Boyanaki, Radava, Vurawara, Wadobuna, Musara, Waraka, Rabaraba, Nakara, Uga; classification given as Oceanic, Papuan Tip Cluster, Nuclear Are-Taupota chain; data from a 2001 SIL Alphabet Design Workshop (village ADW), no dialect differentiation stated. Same languoid as glottocode ghay1237.

sources.note: Sec. 84 'Stress', p. 475, is a Papuan-Tip-Cluster-wide survey remark: stress is phonemic in Kilivila, Muyuw, Budibud, Misima (probably Nimowa, Sud-Est); 'In all of the languages of PTC it seems that stress is predictable within certain word-classes, notably kinship nouns and verbs' (stress moves one syllable rightward with kin plural and object suffixes). Nothing specific to Boanaki/Ghayavi; no placement rule given.
